Turkey.text: Black Sea towns renamed themselves after it: Kadahor became Çaykara and Mapavri became Çayeli (çay is tea).
Turkey.evidence: some towns in the Black Sea region changed their names so as to include the word çay (tea), such as the towns of Kadahor and Mapavri, which became, respectively, Çaykara and Çayeli.

Ireland.text: Irish breakfast tea is almost never called that in Ireland, and is drunk all day.
Ireland.evidence: The tea is virtually never referred to as "breakfast tea" (except as the name of specific blends produced by Barry's, Bewley's, Thompson's and the British brand Twinings) and is drunk throughout the day.

Azerbaijan.text: In matchmaking, tea served without sugar means a marriage is unlikely; with sugar, there will be a wedding.
Azerbaijan.evidence: Tea in Azerbaijan is also served during matchmaking. After the negotiations by matchmakers are complete, the maid will bring out tea. If the tea is served without sugar, that is a sign that the chances for marriage agreement are very low; conversely, if tea is served with sugar, it means that there will be a wedding.

United Kingdom.text: A 1731 patriotic ballad, "The Roast Beef of Old England", sneered at tea as foreign and un-English.
United Kingdom.evidence: When the popular English patriotic ballad "The Roast Beef of Old England" was written in 1731, it portrayed tea (as well as coffee) as foreign and un-English

Pakistan.text: The bestseller Three Cups of Tea takes its title from a Balti proverb: by the third cup, you become family.
Pakistan.evidence: The name for Three Cups of Tea, a bestselling 2007 book by American mountaineer and educator Greg Mortenson, is taken from the Balti proverb in northern Pakistan: "The first time you share tea with a Balti, you are a stranger. The second time you take tea, you are an honored guest. The third time you share a cup of tea, you become family..."

Iran.text: Iranians traditionally pour it into a saucer and put a lump of rock sugar in the mouth before drinking.
Iran.evidence: Iranians traditionally drink tea by pouring it into a saucer and putting a lump of rock sugar (nabāt) in the mouth before drinking the tea.

Russia.text: In the 1630s a Russian envoy first refused a Mongol khan's gift of 250 pounds of tea, seeing no use for dead leaves.
Russia.evidence: According to Jeremiah Curtin, it was possibly in 1636 that Vassili Starkov was sent as envoy to the Altan Khan of the Khalkha. As a gift to the Tsar, he was given 250 pounds of tea. Starkov at first refused, seeing no use for a load of dead leaves, but the Khan insisted.

Morocco.text: A proverb says its three glasses of mint tea are bitter as life, strong as love and soothing as death.
Morocco.evidence: Traditionally, the tea is served three times. ... described in this famous Maghrebi proverb: The first glass is as bitter as life, the second is as strong as love, the third is as soothing as death.

New Zealand.text: Captain Cook and early settlers used mānuka leaves as a tea substitute and called the plant "tea tree".
New Zealand.evidence: Captain Cook and early New Zealand settlers used mānuka (Leptospermum scoparium) as a substitute for tea, and would refer to it as "tea tree".

Chile.text: A 1767 tax on yerba mate, raised to build a Santiago bridge, pushed Chile's working class to drink tea instead.
Chile.evidence: In 1767, the authorities of the Kingdom of Chile created a tax on yerba mate, a very popular drink at the time, with the purpose of financing the construction of the Cal y Canto de Santiago bridge, thus increasing the cost of this concoction, for which the working class was forced to drink tea instead, as a cheaper alternative.
